title: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats
description: James Talarico speaks on election night
body:
James Talarico speaks on election night in Austin, Texas. Talarico won his race for U.S. Senate by 12 percentage points overall, but when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.   It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.   But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.   
   How young voters powered Democrats to victory    Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.   However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.   The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.   
   Explaining the massive shift from 2024   When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.   But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.   
   Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.   The young voters Trump lost    Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.   
   Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.     Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.   How the election results broke down by age     Loading... 
   The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.   "The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."   Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.   
   "I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."   By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.   "Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.   
   "They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

schema.headline: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats

title: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
description: New Zealand Prime Minister and National
body:
New Zealand Prime Minister and National Party leader, Christopher Luxon addresses party faithful in Auckland, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov.7, 2026.
                
                    Alex Robertson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Robertson/AP
    

   
   WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.   The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.   
   The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.   Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.   The conservative bloc has a simpler route to victory, but results could change   Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.   With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.   
   Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.   Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.   Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.   Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins addresses party faithful in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026.
                
                    Mark Tantrum/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Tantrum/AP
    

   
   Incumbent Luxon urges people to 'calm down' and enjoy a break from politics   "I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.   Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.   Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.   Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong poses for a portrait outside Parliament in Wellington, New Zealand, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.
                
                    Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP
    

   
   The vote was a slap for both major parties   New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.   
   The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.   National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.   However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.   Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.   The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.   Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.   Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.   Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

title: Texas's 'Blue Tsunami' has former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke 'over the moon'
description: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big
body:
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big in Texas in the midterms.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:  While Texas' populist roots may have laid the foundation for Democratic victories in the state, they weren't the only factor that helped Texas Democrats win on Tuesday. Former Texas congressman and presidential candidate Beto O'Rourke has helped pave the way for Democrat victories in the Lone Star State. You might remember his 2018 bid to unseat longstanding Republican Senator Ted Cruz. Ultimately, he lost by just a few percentage points. In 2022, he ran against Governor Greg Abbott and again lost, that time by only a slightly larger margin. Beto O'Rourke joins us now. Welcome.BETO O'ROURKE: It's good to be with you.SCHMITZ: So I feel like you have been out of the national spotlight for a while, but perhaps that's because you've been hard at work on the ground there in Texas mobilizing voters. Tell us about that.O'ROURKE: After the Senate race, we asked ourselves, what would it take to win in Texas? And from that, we started a group called Powered By People, and it's thousands of folks - many of whom volunteered on that Senate race - who get trained as volunteer deputy registrars, meet young people in person, get them registered and then, importantly, stay in touch with them and help them overcome the obstacles in a state that makes it harder than any other in the nation for young people to register and to vote, to help them participate in our politics.SCHMITZ: Young folks showed up big time for Democrats this cycle. An NBC exit poll shows that 79% of voters under the age of 30 voted for Talarico. What do you think appealed to that demographic?O'ROURKE: I think, first and foremost, James Talarico, who described this contest as not between a Democrat and a Republican or right versus left, but top versus bottom. When I spend time on these college campuses or at (inaudible) or clubs with young people as we help them to get registered and I ask them what's important to them, they are absolutely disgusted with the concentration of wealth and privilege and power in this country. They ask me about the Epstein files and say, you know, how can the wealthiest, most powerful men rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity? How is it that we're at war again in the Middle East? Why are we complicit in this genocide in Gaza? Why is no one doing anything about these things?And then at home in Texas, the minimum wage is 7.25. It's the hardest state in the nation in which to see a doctor, and schoolteachers are working two or three jobs to make ends meet. These aren't Republican or Democrat issues. They're issues of basic justice, and I think that young people have the most acute sense of what is right or wrong. They are impatient with excuses or equivocation or blaming it on one party or another. They want solutions, and they want people to deliver.SCHMITZ: That's interesting. I mean, this is something that we spoke with our previous guest, David Griscom - he's an author in Texas - about, that economic populism was one of the reasons that James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won both the Senate and gubernatorial election. Is there anything that Democrats can learn from how this played out and what really matters to Texans?O'ROURKE: I think the takeaway is it is incredibly important for Democrats now in power to deliver for the people they represent in ways that they can feel immediately. So raising the minimum wage - if you're working for $7.25 an hour, you're probably working two or three of those jobs to make ends meet. Raising that minimum wage will be felt immediately.You know, if you can't afford to see a doctor right now, and you're suffering as a result of that, being able to, through Medicaid expansion, see a provider - that's going to change your life immediately. And the follow-on effects of being able to afford tuition or down payment on a home or an automobile, these are significant material differences in people's lives.And so we have high expectations for Gina and James. And really, as you probably know, every single statewide office was won by a Democrat. The Democrats also picked a majority in the state House. They now have the opportunity to deliver for people. And so while we're excited and we're celebrating their victories, we're also understanding there's accountability, responsibility, and the clock is ticking.SCHMITZ: You obviously had a lot to do with this popularity of Democrats that we are seeing right now. I mean, you, of course, ran for Senate. You ran for governor. You lost time and time again for both of those races. But a lot in the background was gained. How is this feeling for you right now, seeing these wins?O'ROURKE: I'm over the moon. I mean, you know, my wife, Amy, and I, in 2016, when Trump won - I happened to be in Congress at the time - we looked at each other and we said, we have got to do something more. What we've been doing so far serving in Congress is insufficient to the task at hand, this threat of authoritarianism and fascism and the rise of this oligarchy in America. We needed to do something.And from that was born this crazy snowball's-chance-in-Texas idea of running for Senate in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1988. And I was joined by hundreds of thousands - and by the end, millions - of my fellow Texans who believed in that dream. And so it wasn't so much, you know, should Beto O'Rourke serve in the Senate or, you know, my name on an office or on the ballot. It is, can we change this state? And by extension, given the outsized importance of Texas, can we change this country?SCHMITZ: Well, Beto O'Rourke, since I've got you here, I should ask you whether you have plans to run for president in 2028.O'ROURKE: No, I don't, but I am going to be involved one way or another. This extraordinary experiment 250 years in the making that is the product of so much service and sacrifice and struggle - all of us must do all that we can to keep it going. So that's my mission. That's what I'm going to be focused on. And wherever I can be useful or helpful, that's where you'll find me.SCHMITZ: That is former Texas Congressman Beto O'Rourke. Thanks so much for joining us.O'ROURKE: Thank you.

title: NPR's Moscow and Beijing correspondents discuss the reaction to U.S. elections abroad
description: The results of the U.S. midterms were closely followed overseas. NPR correspondents in Moscow and Beijing discuss how the elections are seen in
body:
The results of the U.S. midterms were closely followed overseas. NPR correspondents in Moscow and Beijing discuss how the elections are seen in the countries they cover.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  Results of the U.S. midterms also created ripples around the world. To discuss the global impact of the election, we're joined now by NPR correspondents Charles Maynes in Moscow and Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Good morning to both of you.CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Morning.JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Charles, if we can start with you, how do you think President Putin will view the midterms?MAYNES: Well, President Putin hasn't spoken directly about the results, but the wider Kremlin approach has been quite transparent, which is to continue actively engaging President Trump. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov this week said Russia is sincerely counting on Trump to continue peace efforts in Ukraine and suggested those efforts had already made some progress, pointing to, for example, Melania Trump's humanitarian work. Also U.S.-led trilateral talks set to take place in Abu Dhabi next week. You know, contrast that with a senior Russian diplomat, the deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, who said Moscow has long viewed Democrats as holding intensely negative views of Russia, so it's obvious who they'd rather deal with.RASCOE: And yet, though, that window of opportunity for dealing with Trump is closing.MAYNES: True. And there's broad acknowledgment that Trump will face more scrutiny from Democrats, including over his dealings with Russia when it comes to Ukraine. You know, at the heart of Trump's recent negotiations with Russia has been this idea that cutting deals with Moscow by offering sanctions relief, for example, that that can unlock Russian concessions over Ukraine, whether that's a good bet or not - and the administration would argue it is working - the midterm results, ironically, may open Russia up to negotiations, simply because Moscow may want to cut a more favorable deal with Trump before this new Congress is seated in January. But, of course, the clock's ticking.RASCOE: And, Jennifer, how is Beijing reacting?PAK: Well, officially, China has been quite measured because, like President Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not going anywhere. So the big question, of course, is is any deal really going to stick with Trump, given that President Xi is really going to be looking for a fourth term next year? He's expected to. So given that being tougher on China is now a bipartisan issue, that question is up in the air.The Chinese foreign ministry have said it's going to be business as usual, that China is willing to work with the U.S. on upholding what Trump and Xi had agreed upon in the earlier two summits this year, which is called the constructive strategic stability. It's quite a mouthful. But essentially, what it means is the two countries have acknowledged they're going to continue to compete, but that there should be some predictability or stability in the relationship.RASCOE: Charles, we've talked about Russia, but I want to turn to Ukraine. How are the results seen there?MAYNES: Yeah. You know, Ukraine is really the flip side of what we were talking about earlier. They're counting the days until this new Democratic-controlled Congress arrives because these incoming congressmen are seen as more sympathetic to Ukraine. It's a point made by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an interview with Jake Tapper on CNN.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: They don't try to balance between us and Russia. They don't afraid to say that Russia is aggressor. They don't want to give our land to Putin. And I think that based on such things, of course, we count on even more support.MAYNES: You know, that said, Zelenskyy is clearly being careful not to antagonize Trump outright, aware, of course, that the president could make life very difficult for Ukrainians, even with the Democrats controlling Congress.RASCOE: President Trump and President Xi are expected to meet later this month in China. What's likely to be on the agenda?PAK: Well, we don't know yet, but this is essentially a trust-building exercise because, despite the pleasantries that have been exchanged between Trump and Xi and the warmth, the U.S. administration in between these summits have continually added more Chinese firms and individuals on blacklists. They've also banned, like, Chinese humanoids, drones from being imported into the U.S., while China, according to the U.S., continues to restrict the flow of rare earth to the U.S. and hasn't really followed through on his purchases of U.S. agricultural goods. So following through on the promises made in the last two summits is essentially going to be the goal.We have heard they've made progress on lowering tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods flowing between the two countries. They've identified which items that are non-sensitive, and that might be easier to push through because of the cost of living became a key issue in the midterms. The areas that are much harder to negotiate on are, for example, Chinese investments in the U.S., the American stance on Taiwan and also guardrails on AI. But the purpose, according to Chinese analysts I've spoken to, of these summits is to build mutual trust because there is just so little right now between the U.S. and China.RASCOE: And, Charles, the two leaders could be joined for the talks by President Putin. If that were to happen, how significant would that be?MAYNES: Well, it could be hugely significant, at least when it comes to Ukraine. A few days ago, Trump held a meeting at the White House with the Kremlin's envoy, a man by the name of Kirill Dmitriev, after which Trump said the U.S. and Russia were closing in on a peace deal for Ukraine that could also impact all of Europe. Let's listen to Trump.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled.MAYNES: Now, Trump has repeatedly overstated his abilities to end this war. But the idea that he and Putin, or perhaps with input from Xi, could negotiate some grand superpower bargain while cutting Ukraine and Europe out of the loop is a fear that's dogged Trump's peace efforts since he returned to office. I think the catch here is that it's even harder now to imagine Ukraine or, for that matter, Europe, accepting those terms, given the midterm results and what's left of Trump's time in office.RASCOE: That's NPR correspondents Charles Maynes in Moscow and Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Thank you so much for joining us.MAYNES: Thank you.RASCOE: You're welcome.(SOUNDBITE OF PURE X'S "YOU'RE IN IT NOW")

title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
description: FILE - President Donald Trump waves alon
body:
FILE - President Donald Trump waves alongside Dana White, president and CEO of UFC, as they arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House, June 14, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Mark Schiefelbein/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Schiefelbein/AP
    

   
   WEST PALM BEACH, Fla.  — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.   Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.   
   White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.   When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."   He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."   Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."   The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.   Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"   
   While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.   Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.   Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.   The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.   The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.   Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.   He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.   
   "It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.   White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

title: Republican consultant discusses what went wrong and what's next for the GOP
description: NPR's Ayesha Rascoe speaks to Hogan Gidley, a Republican consultant and former White House Deputy Press Secretary during the first Trump admini
body:
NPR's Ayesha Rascoe speaks to Hogan Gidley, a Republican consultant and former White House Deputy Press Secretary during the first Trump administration, about the GOP's post-midterm strategy.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  January 20, 2025, was a blustery, bitterly cold day in Washington. President Trump, in his inaugural address, heralded a tide of change sweeping the country, thanking Black and Hispanic voters in particular. Less than two years later, another tide has swept in the opposite direction, electing Democrats in Republican strongholds from South Carolina to Kansas. So what went wrong for the GOP? And what's next for the party?We're joined now by Hogan Gidley. He's a longtime Republican consultant, and he was White House deputy press secretary during the first Trump administration. Hogan, thanks for being here.HOGAN GIDLEY: Great to be with you. Thanks so much for the time.RASCOE: What happened to that expanded MAGA coalition that we mentioned? Why did Hispanics and young people, even young white men, turn away from the GOP?GIDLEY: Polling suggests that their anger at the war and that their anger at prices had a lot to do with the way they voted. Because a lot of the things the Trump administration did - from no tax on tips to no tax on overtime and no tax on Social Security, doubling the child tax credit, the lowest number in crime we've seen over a century, the highest wages we've seen, the lowest number of unemployment we've ever seen - all those things are very exciting. Those things the American people like. What they didn't like were the war and prices.RASCOE: Well, does Trump need to make any changes in his behavior? Because people are not happy with the direction of the country. They do not feel like Trump cares about their individual problems. So does Trump need to make any changes?GIDLEY: Well, I'll tell you something that stood out to me that may answer this question. The mere fact that Donald Trump got elected to the White House and has been the driving force in politics for 10 years, based on the fact that he is the one who is viewed by the American people to be listening to them finally after decades of government officials and candidates and officeholders not listening to them - someone who was known to be the voice of the American people - the fact that that has shifted in their opinion and their perception is something that they'll have to address. How that looks moving forward, though, I think, is that there will be a massive - and this is my silver lining from the election - a massive overreach by Democrats and a misread of what the American people truly want from this last election.RASCOE: Well, it sounds like what you're saying is that Republicans have to depend on missteps by Democrats. But what is the Republican plan? What is the...GIDLEY: No.RASCOE: ...Republican agenda?GIDLEY: I think that's what's being formulated. It's...RASCOE: OK.GIDLEY: ...Reestablishing an understanding.RASCOE: Would you agree that they're a bit in the wilderness and they have to figure a way out?GIDLEY: I wouldn't say they're in the wilderness. I'd say they're on the edge of the forest, wondering, what do we need to do before we step out into the field? Because they have the White House right now. They are in control of that. So it's obvious the American people still want Republicans to have some say. The question is - what are they saying, and how are they saying it? Democrats didn't run on anything other than being against Donald Trump. What's their agenda? I don't know what their agenda is either.RASCOE: There's been a backlash to some of President Trump's immigration enforcement policies. Now the architect of Trump's immigration push, Stephen Miller, has been elevated to White House chief of staff. What does that tell you?GIDLEY: It tells me that the administration wants to make sure that continuity is key heading into one of the most tumultuous times, most likely in our nation's history, because we face an onslaught of a weaponized Congress the likes of which we have never seen in this country against Donald Trump, with hoax after hoax, with impeachment attempt after impeachment attempt. They're going to continue to move that onslaught against Donald Trump and his administration. Stephen Miller was part and parcel with defending Donald Trump in the first term, as was I. And so Stephen's ready for that type of fight.RASCOE: But what does that say to Latinos, who swung 21 points toward Democratic House candidates? And part of that, when you look at polls, was because of unmet promises to lower prices and because of the deportation tactics.GIDLEY: I've not seen any indication of deportation tactics being the driving cause...RASCOE: It's a part of it.GIDLEY: ...Of the backlash.RASCOE: It's not the - it's definitely a part of it.GIDLEY: You may not like the images that come out of that enforcement. The problem is - or, I guess, the success is - we now have net-zero or net-negative migration into this country. The American people have seen a reduction in crime the likes of which no one thought possible. Stephen Miller was obviously an architect of that and a driver of that. And so I expect more of it to continue moving into the next two years.RASCOE: That's Republican consultant Hogan Gidley. Thank you so much for joining us.GIDLEY: Thank you so much. Appreciate it.

title: Historically red state legislatures have flipped. Here's what's on their agenda
description: Democrats made sweeping gains in state legislatures across the country. We look at North Carolina and Arizona to see what that could mean.
body:
Democrats made sweeping gains in state legislatures across the country. We look at North Carolina and Arizona to see what that could mean.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  Democrats made sweeping gains in state legislatures around the country, and they'll be looking to reverse recent history. In 2010, Republicans dominated state elections and used that power to advance their agenda for over a decade. So what are Democrats going to do this time around? We're going to hear from two of those states now, from two of our member stations with Colin Campbell of WUNC in North Carolina and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ in Arizona. Welcome.COLIN CAMPBELL, BYLINE: Thanks, Ayesha.WAYNE SCHUTSKY, BYLINE: Hi.RASCOE: Both your states have had Democratic governors and heavily Republican legislatures. Let's start in North Carolina. Colin, what's changed there?CAMPBELL: So Republicans here have had what they call working supermajorities for much of the past decade. That's enough votes, sometimes with the help of a Democrat or two, to override most of the Democratic governors' vetoes. That's allowed them to pass new abortion restrictions after the fall of Roe v. Wade, expand private school vouchers and also gerrymander congressional maps.But on Tuesday, Democrats not only flipped the state House but will have a comfortable majority in that chamber. In the Senate, there's still one election that's being counted - could be just a one-seat majority for the GOP or a tie. If it's a tie, that would be broken by the Democratic lieutenant governor.RASCOE: So what could change for North Carolinians? What are Democrats hoping to do?CAMPBELL: You know, if Democrats manage to control both chambers, that could mean a rollback of abortion restrictions or reversing power grabs that have weakened the governor's office, and a whole lot more. If the Democrats end up coming up short in the state Senate, we get divided government, and it's unclear what, if anything, gets done. Regardless of how it shakes out, Democratic Governor Josh Stein is already calling for lawmakers from both parties to cooperate on issues like affordability.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JOSH STEIN: What I heard from the people of North Carolina is, do something for us, focus on our issues, listen to our concerns and work together. Don't be so focused on the partisan divide. Focus on producing for people.CAMPBELL: A lot of the North Carolina voters I've talked with want to see that bipartisan progress.RASCOE: Now to Wayne Schutsky in Phoenix. Bigger change there - Republicans had controlled both chambers of the legislature, but now it's a Democratic trifecta.SCHUTSKY: That's right. With Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs easily winning reelection, Democrats will now hold both legislative chambers and the governor's office for the first time since 1966. And this was really part of that larger blue wave we saw across the country. I mean, just for example, not in the legislature, but even the Republican clerk of court in Maricopa County, the biggest county in the state, lost to a 19-year-old Democrat who's a philosophy student at ASU, who will now oversee hundreds of court employees.So for years, the Republican-controlled legislature has blocked Hobbs, the Democratic governor, on her agenda, and she spent the last four decades playing defense, setting a state record with more than 500 vetoes. But now she'll be able to actually initiate changes that she wants to see in the state.RASCOE: And what kind of changes are Democrats considering?SCHUTSKY: Well, for years, Hobbs has tried to provide financial relief to Arizonans through things like rent and utility assistance, relief for first-time homebuyers, and increasing the amount the state spends to help families afford childcare. For instance, she sought around a hundred million to help with childcare assistance but only got a fraction of that, and we still have over 15,000 kids on the wait list for that program.One thing we do know Democrats are going to do is try and crack down on Arizona's school voucher program, which is one of the biggest in the country. She sought to scale it back for years, as we've seen reports on families using public dollars for non-education items, things like jewelry and even lingerie. So this has been a huge issue, and Senate Republican John Kavanagh actually acknowledged to me in an interview that his party missed an opportunity to address some concerns about those vouchers, which we call ESAs here.JOHN KAVANAGH: I think that in the area of, like, ESA reform, that was something that the voters very much wanted and that we weren't going along. I mean, that's one area that was problematic.SCHUTSKY: Still, Republicans tell me they think their losses still had more to do with President Trump than anything they actually did.RASCOE: Well, Colin, can you sum up a little about where there could be big changes in other states?CAMPBELL: Yeah. This year's blue wave definitely had ripple effects through a lot of state Houses. Going into the election, Republicans had control of 28 state legislatures. Democrats had 18. A few others were divided. Now Democrats will control more than the GOP. The National Conference of State Legislatures projects this time around, Democrats will control 25, Republicans will control 21. In addition to that trifecta in Arizona, Democrats have new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. In Nevada, they got a trifecta by winning the governor's office, and we'll see what happens here in North Carolina with this vote count.In terms of some of the issues and what this all means, well, several of the states that haven't yet expanded Medicaid could do it next year, and that would obviously give more people access to health care. North Carolina here is one of several states where Democrats are already talking about increasing the minimum wage. And in other places, Democrats managed to flip one of the chambers. That number includes Texas and Georgia. So depending on how you look at it, that could be gridlock or Democrats putting the brakes on the sweeping powers that Republicans have had for years now. Of course, some Republicans, like the Republican state leadership committee that supports their campaigns - they're vowing to take back seats two years from now in the next round.RASCOE: That's Colin Campbell in Raleigh and Wayne Schutsky in Phoenix. Thank you so much for joining us.CAMPBELL: Thank you.SCHUTSKY: Yeah, thanks for having me.

title: Week in politics: Democrats plan for the next Congress, Trump's new Chief of Staff
description:
Democrats plans for the next Congress, where they'll hold significant majorities in both chambers.
Meanwhile, President Trump signals his plans
body:
Democrats plans for the next Congress, where they'll hold significant majorities in both chambers.
Meanwhile, President Trump signals his plans by promoting Stephen Miller as his new Chief of Staff.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  The midterms were chock full of surprises.(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)JAMES TALARICO: We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.(CHEERING)ABDUL EL-SAYED: My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.(CHEERING)EL-SAYED: And I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.(CHEERING)KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS: And no matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia.(CHEERING)RASCOE: That's Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will become the country's first Black female governor. Some other surprises - the senators-elect from Michigan and Texas, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, just three of the many Democrats who gave victory speeches last week. NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson is with us now. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Can you put this Democratic sweep into perspective?LIASSON: It's the biggest shift in power since the 1974 elections right after Watergate. There's still more than a dozen races in the House left to be called, but the Democrats could have as big as an 80-seat majority in the House next January. And in the Senate, they have 54 seats now, but Mississippi and Alaska are still left to be called, and that could end up being 56 seats. Democrats also won up and down the ballot in red states. Texas was the most dramatic example of that - the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state lawmakers.There are also six new Democratic state trifectas. That means that Democrats will control both legislative chambers and the governor's mansion in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Those are big states that are important for the 2028 presidential elections.And if that doesn't convince you of the scope of the wins, just consider what some Republicans said about it. Texas senator said - Ted Cruz called it a Watergate-level repudiation. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis called it close to an extinction-level event for Republicans. And one of the most descriptive lines came from Henry Olsen of the Ethics and Public Policy Center in a column for The Washington Post, where he wrote, the midterms were not just an earthquake, they were a continent-wide rupture of the Earth's crust, allowing molten lava to spill out across the nation and burn Republican bastions to the ground.RASCOE: Well, that is quite the image.LIASSON: (laughter).RASCOE: So what happened to the voters who broke for Trump in 2024?LIASSON: Well, the Trump coalition fell apart and turned back to Democrats. The groups that had moved toward him in 2024 - Latinos were the biggest swing - moved back to the Democrats. White non-college voters, young Black men, especially in the once-solid Republican South, African American voters, who are angry like everyone else about the war and the economy, were particularly angry that the Supreme Court had weakened the Voting Rights Act and allowed Republicans to gerrymander away congressional districts long held by Black representatives. Those voters turned out in huge numbers, even better than in the 2024 presidential election.RASCOE: OK. So with the incoming Congress, what does the Democratic Caucus look like? And what are they saying that they will do?LIASSON: Well, yeah. You know, there was a lot made this year about left-wing candidates winning, and the Democratic Socialists of America did increase their numbers in the House from four to eight. But they were not the majority makers. The majority makers were centrist Democrats who won in red states and rural places.And Hakeem Jeffries, who's poised to be the next House speaker, said he expects the caucus to work together to try to find the, quote, "highest common denominator." And he has the gift of a big majority, so he won't be beholden to any one group inside the Democratic ranks the way Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson was because he only had a three-seat majority.Democrats say what they want to do is focus first on affordability, pass bills that will lower prices for Americans on housing, healthcare, food, gas - hope that Trump will sign them.Second priority is accountability. There are going to be a lot of investigations. Democrats want to tell a story about the connection between high prices and corruption.RASCOE: And how has the president been taking all of this?LIASSON: Well, Donald Trump says different things at different times, as he often does. But he has said he's willing to work with Democrats to make deals. But if they can't agree, he'll become Mr. Veto.But he's also done something that better communicates how he's planning to go forward. He promoted Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff. Miller is the deputy chief of staff now, and he has promoted the hardest of hard lines on any number of issues, primarily mass deportations. He believes in unchecked executive power. And by choosing Miller, Trump is showing that he is ready for a lot of confrontation with an opposition Congress.RASCOE: That's NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson. Thank you so much.LIASSON: You're welcome.
